### SUMMARY

Fully explored the FirewallGuard AI frontend (React/TypeScript SPA): read all 30 component files, the 3 lib modules (api.ts, types.ts, router.ts), and the main App.tsx. The app uses a simple hash-based router, a dual-mode sidebar (tenant vs superadmin/operator), and a `ModalHost` context for confirm/prompt dialogs. The "Security Analytics" sidebar nav item at `/security-analytics` renders `FindingsExplorer` (same as `/findings`), while the actual analytics dashboard is `Trends.tsx` at `/analytics`. All API calls go through a centralized client with automatic JWT refresh on 401.

- `frontend/src/App.tsx:1-433` — main app shell, routing, sidebar, TopBar, ProfileMenu

### RISKS

- **`/security-analytics` is a misleading label**: It renders the same `FindingsExplorer` component as `/findings`, not a distinct analytics page. Users clicking "Security Analytics" may expect charts/trends but get the findings list. Mitigation: either rename the nav item or create a dedicated analytics dashboard.
- **No TypeScript strict null checks visible**: Many components use `as` casts and `any` types (e.g., `demoAnalysis as unknown as Analysis` at `App.tsx:126`, `(result.snapshot as Record<string, unknown>)` in CelBuilder). Mitigation: enable `strict: true` in tsconfig and fix type holes.
- **Polling loop unbounded**: `UploadPanel.tsx:41-44` polls for 120 iterations at 1.5s each (3 min) with no user cancellation. Mitigation: add AbortController support.
- **No lazy loading / code splitting**: All 30 components are imported synchronously at the top of `App.tsx`. Mitigation: use `React.lazy` for route-level components.

### SUMMARY

I read all 15 FirewallGuard modules to document the full analysis pipeline. The engine ingests SonicWall TSR files (GUI or API format), normalizes them, parses 18+ configuration sections into a structured snapshot, runs 40+ evidence-gated detection rules across three catalogs (core, parity, informational), enriches with PSIRT firmware intelligence, correlates findings into multi-stage attack paths, computes a 0–100 security score with A–F grade, detects configuration drift between two snapshots, and generates PDF/CSV/JSON reports — all as a DB-agnostic, deterministic Python library.

### EVIDENCE

- `backend/firewallguard/pipeline.py:1-172` — Orchestrator: `analyze_text()` entry point, `analyze_snapshot()` runs rules → firmware intel → correlation → scoring. Calls `registry.run_all(snapshot)`, `get_intel().evaluate()`, `correlate()`, `score_findings()`. Handles suppressions, system_filter_fn, and extra_findings_fn.
- `backend/firewallguard/tsr/reader.py:1-109` — `TSRDocument` class parses `#Section_START`/`#Section_END` markers with a stack-based splitter. `Section` dataclass with `kv()` for key:value extraction, `value()` for single-key lookup, `find()`, `find_all()`, `find_like()`, `first_like()`, `nth_like()`. `iter_blocks()` generator for repeating record layouts.
- `backend/firewallguard/tsr/parser.py:1-572` — `parse_tsr()` orchestrates 18 section parsers: system, licenses, administration, SNMP, interfaces, zones, address objects, services, access rules, NAT policies, VPN, SSL VPN, user settings, local users, certificates, HA, security services, logging. Each parser is defensive (empty structure on missing section). Defines `_to_bool`, `_to_int`, `_split_ifaces` helpers. Access rules parsed via `_RULE_HEADER` regex with zone→zone notation. VPN uses `--- SA N ---` block headers. Calls `enrich_snapshot` from parser_ext.
- `backend/firewallguard/tsr/parser_ext.py:1-177` — Six additional parsers: `parse_firewall_settings` (stealth mode, SYN/UDP/ICMP flood protection, DDoS, FTP bounce, TCP handshake enforcement), `parse_local_users_detailed` (per-user MFA detection via OTP/TOTP regex), `parse_wlan` (SSID/encryption), `parse_cfs` (HTTPS filtering, reputation, safe search), `parse_performance` (CPU samples), `parse_auth_servers` (RADIUS/TACACS+ accounting, login uniqueness). `enrich_snapshot()` folds all into snapshot.
- `backend/firewallguard/tsr/normalize.py:1-307` — Dual-format normalization. `detect_tsr_format()` classifies input as "api" (whitespace-collapsed) or "gui" by comparing own-line `_START` marker ratio. `normalize_api_tsr()`: restores section markers from `sonicos_sections.txt` catalog, re-segments run-on key:value lines via longest-suffix matching against `sonicos_keys.txt`, reconstructs record blocks (table markers, dash headers, member lines, access-rule headers, VPN SA headers), de-merges interface lists via token regex, fixes numeric colon-spacing, re-spaces model/firmware/VPN crypto tokens. `normalize_tsr()` returns `(text, format)` tuple.
- `backend/firewallguard/rules/engine.py:1-154` — Core rule engine. `Finding` dataclass: 22 fields including rule_id, severity, evidence, likelihood/impact/exposure (1-5), exploitability property (weighted: 0.4×L + 0.35×E + 0.25×I), object_name/object_type for per-object reporting. `Rule` dataclass: id, title, severity, category, check(snapshot)→[Finding]. `RuleRegistry` with `register()`, `retire()`, `active_rules()`, `rule()` decorator, `run_all()` (runs all active rules, sorts by severity). Module-level `registry` singleton. `SEVERITY_WEIGHTS` dict for scoring.
- `backend/firewallguard/rules/catalog.py:1-918` — Core detection catalog (~25 rules). Categories: Management Security (FW-MGT-001 through FW-MGT-008 covering WAN exposure, password policy, lockout, MFA, default admin name, SNMP v1/v2c, API MD5, audit logging), Firewall Security (FW-SVC-001 through FW-SVC-009 covering DPI-SSL, IPS/GAV/anti-spyware expiry, IPS prevention tiers, Capture ATP, performance profile, zone enforcement, GAV outbound), VPN Security (FW-VPN-001 through FW-VPN-003: weak IKE/IPsec crypto, aggressive mode, DH groups), SSL VPN (FW-SSL-001 through FW-SSL-003: WAN exposure, multi-zone, web mgmt over SSLVPN). All rules evidence-gated. Reuses compliance constant mappings (CIS, NIST CSF, PCI DSS, ISO 27001).
- `backend/firewallguard/rules/catalog_parity.py:1-910` — Parity detection catalog (~30+ rules organized by check-code families: ACR, AOB, SVC, NAT, IPSEC, SEC, FW, AUTH, WLAN, SNMP, MGMT, SSLVPN, SYSTEM, DHCP). Per-object rules emit one Finding per affected access rule/address object/NAT policy/VPN policy with `object_name`/`object_type`. Covers: WAN allow any-service (ACR-007), disabled rules (ACR-008), unused objects (AOB-003, SVC-004, NAT-003), duplicates (AOB-001, SVC-001), weak IKE/Phase2/PFS (IPSEC-001/003/006), disabled VPN policies (IPSEC-008), per-zone service gaps, stealth mode, SYN/UDP/ICMP flood protection, WAN DDoS, MFA coverage, WLAN open SSIDs, SSLVPN cipher/portal timeout.
- `backend/firewallguard/rules/catalog_info.py:1-143` — Informational inventory checks (~11 rules, all Info severity, all IDs suffixed -I001). Covers: access rules total, address objects total, service objects total, NAT policies total, VPN policies total, local users count, IPS license, GAV license, firmware & platform, wireless SSID count. All use shared `_info()` helper; contribute zero score penalty.
- `backend/firewallguard/intelligence/firmware.py:1-137` — PSIRT intelligence. `FirmwareIntelligence` class loads `data/psirt.json`. `Advisory` dataclass with advisory_id, CVE list, CVSS, affected_lo/hi, fixed_in, generations. `_normalise()` converts "SonicOS 7.3.0-7012-R4521" → (7,3,0,7012) 4-tuple. `_in_range()` does SonicOS-aware version comparison. `evaluate()` matches firmware against advisories filtering by generation (Gen6/Gen7/Gen8), checks EoL status per model. `get_intel()` returns singleton. Results sorted by CVSS descending.
- `backend/firewallguard/intelligence/correlation.py:1-149` — Attack path correlation. `AttackPath` dataclass: path_id, name, severity, stages list, narrative, contributing_rules, recommended_priority. Four deterministic patterns: AP-001 (Internet→management-plane takeover via WAN management + firmware vulnerability + weak auth), AP-002 (SSL VPN→management escalation via WAN-exposed SSLVPN + web mgmt over SSLVPN + no admin MFA), AP-003 (encrypted-traffic blind spot: DPI-SSL off + reduced inline engines), AP-004 (flat-network lateral movement: permissive inter-zone rules + uninspected zones). Uses rule-id membership (`_present()` set-check).
- `backend/firewallguard/analytics/scoring.py:1-118` — Scoring engine. Starts at 100, subtracts `weight × sqrt(count)` per severity capped at per-severity maximums (Critical:60, High:40, Medium:24, Low:12, Info:0). Hard caps: any Critical finding → max 59 (grade F), any High → max 79 (grade C). Grade scale: ≥100=Secure, 90-99=A, 80-89=B, 70-79=C, 60-69=D, <60=F. `score_findings()` returns score, grade, grade_label, severity_counts, category_counts, penalty_by_severity, total_penalty. `exploitability_distribution()` counts findings per exploitability band.
- `backend/firewallguard/analytics/drift.py:1-247` — Drift detection. `DriftAlert` dataclass: category, change_type (added/removed/changed/upgraded/downgraded), severity, title, detail, previous_state, current_state, identifier. `detect_drift(prev_snapshot, curr_snapshot)` runs 7 comparison dimensions: access rules (keyed by src_zone→dst_zone|service|src→dst|name), NAT policies (orig_/trans_ fields), VPN policies (name/SA), security services (5 toggles with severity calibrated per field), firmware version, admin settings (6 fields), interfaces (add/remove/rezone). All comparisons key-based with enabled-state diffing.
- `backend/firewallguard/report/generator.py:1-575` — Report generation. PDF via ReportLab Platypus: `build_executive_pdf()` (title, score band with grade/score chips, device table, posture summary, firmware intelligence summary, findings summary table), `build_technical_pdf()` (findings index with clickable anchors, per-finding detail cards with evidence/impact/remediation/verification tables, attack path analysis with stage narratives), `build_comparison_pdf()` (score comparison table, change summary with new/resolved counts, side-by-side finding presence). CSV export: `export_findings_csv()` (14 columns). JSON export: `export_json()` with optional snapshot inclusion. `to_csv_string()` for in-memory. Configurable branding (company_name, primary_color, contact) via optional dict. Consistent `_PALETTE` colors.
- `backend/firewallguard/cli.py:1-82` — Standalone CLI via `argparse`. Two subcommands: `analyze TSR.wri [--out OUTDIR]` (prints device info, score, findings summary, attack paths; optionally writes executive PDF, technical PDF, findings CSV, analysis JSON), `drift OLD NEW [--json]` (prints drift alerts with severity counts; optionally full JSON). Reads files with `utf-8`/`replace` errors. `python -m firewallguard.cli`.

### CHANGES

None.

### RISKS

- **API normalization: token de-merging is lossy.** The `_demerge_interfaces()` and crypto-token regex heuristics (`backend/firewallguard/tsr/normalize.py:159-179`) may fail on unusual interface names or custom DH group names, causing false positives/negatives in rules that depend on those fields. Mitigation: the module-level note in the UI should be retained; periodic validation against real API TSRs is needed.
- **TSR section variance across SonicOS releases.** The parser assumes specific section names and KV layouts (`backend/firewallguard/tsr/parser.py:48-572`); a new SonicOS release could rename sections or change record formats, causing silent parse failures (empty structures) rather than errors. Mitigation: parser test corpus should cover 6.5.x, 7.0.x, and 7.3.x TSRs across TZ/NSa/NSsp/NSv platforms.
- **PSIRT data staleness.** The firmware intelligence (`backend/firewallguard/intelligence/firmware.py:71-73`) loads a static JSON file; if not refreshed, advisories will be missing, producing false assurance. Mitigation: the scheduled refresh mentioned in the docstring should be implemented and monitored.
- **Correlation is limited to 4 hardcoded patterns.** `backend/firewallguard/intelligence/correlation.py:42-149` — if new rule IDs are added or renumbered, the pattern precondition sets will miss valid attack paths. Mitigation: consider making patterns data-driven from a separate config.
- **Square-root damped scoring may under-weight tail findings.** `backend/firewallguard/analytics/scoring.py:85-89` — the sqrt curve means 100 Low findings contribute the same penalty as ~10 Low findings. 2. **Configuration** (TSR upload via `POST /customers/{customer_id}/tsrs` or API connect via `POST /devices/connect`): The TSR serial must match the pre-registered serial. On match, the device is marked `configured=True` and its model/firmware are updated from the TSR. For API connect, no prior registration is needed — the device can be auto-registered from the TSR's serial.
3. **Analysis**: After configuration, the `upload_tsr` endpoint parses the TSR, saves it to object storage, creates a `Tsr` + `Analysis` (status=queued), and dispatches a Celery task (`dispatch_analysis`). The worker runs the full `firewallguard.pipeline`, applies CEL custom rules and suppressions, normalizes API TSRs, syncs findings to the `Finding` table, computes drift against the previous analysis, and fires alerts.

**HOW TSRs ARE UPLOADED, PARSED, AND FINDINGS GENERATED**
1. Upload: `POST /customers/{customer_id}/tsrs` requires a `device_id`. The TSR file is read, size-checked (max from settings), and decoded to UTF-8.
2. Parsing: `parse_tsr` from `firewallguard.tsr.parser` produces a structured dict including system info (serial, model, firmware). The serial is validated against the registered device; on mismatch the upload is rejected.
3. The TSR is saved to object storage (`save_tsr`), a `Tsr` row is created, and an `Analysis` (status=queued) is dispatched to Celery (or run inline).
4. The pipeline (`run_analysis_inline`): loads the TSR from storage, normalizes (GUI vs API format), runs the Python rule catalog + CEL custom rules, applies suppressions/severity overrides, scores the results, and persists via `sync_findings`. The `sync_findings` function reconciles pipeline findings into `Finding` rows using composite fingerprints (rule_id::object_type::object_name), auto-reopening fixed findings on re-detect and auto-resolving vanished ones.

**HOW API-BASED TSR COLLECTION WORKS**
1. The `POST /devices/connect` endpoint accepts hostname, port, username, password, and either a `device_id` (existing) or `customer_id` (new device).
2. `_run_api_flow` first checks for an active configurable `ApiFlowConfig`. If present, it calls `api_flow.run_flow` which executes the DB-stored multi-step HTTP flow (auth → export TSR → logout) using stdlib urllib. If no config, it falls back to the legacy hardcoded `SonicOSClient` which performs the same 3-step Gen7 flow.
3. The downloaded TSR bytes are identified (serial, model, firmware) via `_identify_from_tsr`.
4. For pre-registered devices, serial validation is enforced; for new devices, a `Device` row is auto-created.
5. Credentials are encrypted via Fernet and stored as `DeviceCredential`.
6. The TSR is ingested via `ingest_tsr_bytes` (same path as uploaded TSRs) — saved to storage, Tsr+Analysis created, and analyzed inline.
7. On-demand pulls (`POST /devices/{device_id}/pull`) reuse saved credentials and enforce license frequency windows (e.g., only one pull per 30 days for monthly licenses).

**HOW SCHEDULING AND AUTOMATED SCANNING WORKS**
1. Each device can have one `Schedule` row (upserted via `PUT /devices/{device_id}/schedule`) with frequency (manual/hourly/daily/weekly/monthly), time-of-day, day-of-week/month, timezone, blackout windows, and enabled/disabled.
2. `scheduler.compute_next_run` computes the next UTC fire time considering frequency, day constraints, and blackout windows.
3. A Celery Beat poller (`run_due_schedules`) iterates enabled schedules whose `next_run_at <= now`, acquires a per-tenant Redis scan slot (`acquire_scan_slot`), and calls `enqueue_scheduled_scan` which dispatches `scheduled_scan_task`.
4. The task calls `pull_and_analyze` which connects via saved DeviceCredential, downloads the TSR, creates Tsr+Analysis, runs the pipeline, and releases the scan slot.
5. Concurrency is limited per tenant via Redis counters (`max_concurrent_scans_per_tenant`), failing open if Redis is down.
6. License frequency windows are enforced for manual pulls (`POST /devices/{device_id}/pull`).

**HOW THE LICENSE/BILLING SYSTEM WORKS**
1. **Plans**: Three default plans (Free, Professional, MSP) are seeded in DB, each with features, pricing tiers (per-frequency), and limits. Superadmins can create/edit/clone/delete plans and assign them to organizations.
2. **Licensing**: Plans are dynamic, stored in the `Plan` table. Organizations have a `plan_id` and `license_allocations` dict tracking {subscription_term: {frequency: count}}. `LicensePurchase` rows record individual purchases with expiry dates, tier info (for MSP), and device counts.
3. **Registration**: When registering a device (`POST /devices`), a specific `license_purchase_id` is required. The endpoint validates that the purchase exists, is not expired, matches the requested frequency, and has remaining device slots.
4. **Purchasing**: `POST /organization/purchase` is additive — it increments license allocations and creates a new `LicensePurchase` row. Supports monthly/yearly subscription terms, MSP tier-based purchasing, and testing plans with short validity.
5. **Stripe**: When configured, `POST /billing/checkout` creates a Stripe Checkout session. The `POST /billing/webhook` receiver processes events (session completed, subscription updated/deleted, payment failed) and updates org state accordingly. Without Stripe (`settings.stripe_api_key` unset), the system runs in local mode — checkout immediately applies the plan.
6. **Free tier**: `_enforce_plan` in analyses.py limits free-tier uploads to `settings.free_tier_upload_limit`. `ensure_free_license` creates a free 30-day license on registration.
7. **Trials**: 14-day Professional trial (`start_trial`); `downgrade_expired_trials` periodically reverts lapsed trials to Free.
8. **Enforcement**: `billing.py`'s `enforce_device_limit`, `enforce_schedule_limit`, `enforce_integration_limit` return HTTP 402 when limits are exceeded.
9. **Retention**: Data retention days vary by plan (config in `settings.retention_days`), with per-org override.

### CHANGES

None.

### RISKS

- **API flow engine uses stdlib urllib only (no connection pooling)**: Each API flow opens a new TLS connection. For large scheduled fleets this could create connection churn. Mitigation: the per-tenant concurrency limit (`max_concurrent_scans_per_tenant`) caps simultaneous connections, and `timeout_seconds` prevents leaking sockets.
- **SAML signature validation is explicitly not implemented**: The docstring warns that signature verification requires xmlsec/python3-saml and is gated behind `settings.saml_verify_signature` (default False). Any production deployment against an untrusted IdP must add this before enabling SAML.
- **System-rule CEL filters are disabled via feature flag**: `evaluate_system_rule_filters` is called in `make_pipeline_hooks` but the system_filter_fn currently returns `set()` unconditionally (the CEL evaluation loop is commented out). When enabled, 68+ CEL conditions would be compiled per scan — performance has not been validated.
- **Stripe webhook uses plain JSON when no secret is configured**: When `stripe_webhook_secret` is unset, the payload is parsed directly without signature verification (`json.loads(payload)`). In production this should always be configured or the endpoint should return 400.

### BLOCKERS

None.

### SUMMARY

I read all 16 specified source files covering the full FirewallGuard AI analysis engine. The system is a modular, defensive pipeline that transforms a raw SonicWall Tech Support Report (TSR) through five stages: **parse → rules → firmware intelligence → correlation → scoring**, producing a JSON-serialisable analysis dictionary consumed by the report generator, drift detector, and CLI. Each module is independently defensive (missing sections produce empty structures, never exceptions). The rule engine uses an evidence-gated model with ~67 detection rules (core catalog + parity + informational), a `Finding` dataclass with exploitability scoring, and CEL support hooks. The normalizer bridges API-format (whitespace-collapsed) TSRs to GUI-equivalent text so a single parser handles both. The scoring algorithm starts at 100 and subtracts square-root-damped severity penalties, capped per band, with Critical findings capping at 59 (grade F) and High at 79 (max C).

### EVIDENCE

- **`backend/firewallguard/tsr/reader.py:1-148`** — `TSRDocument` class splits raw TSR text into ordered `Section` dataclass instances using `#<NAME>_START` / `#<NAME>_END` regex markers. Supports nested sections via a stack. Provides `find()`, `find_all()`, `find_like()`, `first_like()`, `nth_like()` navigation. `iter_blocks()` helper yields `(match, block_lines)` tuples for repeating record layouts. `Section.kv()` extracts first-occurrence `Key : Value` pairs.

- **`backend/firewallguard/tsr/parser.py:542-572`** — `parse_tsr()` is the orchestrator: creates a `TSRDocument`, calls ~16 `parse_*` functions, then delegates to `enrich_snapshot()` from `parser_ext` for extended fields. Returns a `Snapshot = Dict[str, Any]` dictionary with keys: `meta, system, licenses, administration, snmp, interfaces, zones, address_objects, services, access_rules, nat_policies, vpn, sslvpn, user_settings, local_users, certificates, ha, security_services, logging`.

- **`backend/firewallguard/tsr/parser_ext.py:1-120`** — `enrich_snapshot()` folds 6 additional sections into the snapshot: `firewall_settings` (stealth mode, flood/DDoS protection, FTP bounce), `local_users_detail` (MFA coverage per user), `wlan` (SSID/encryption), `cfs` (content filtering detail), `performance` (CPU samples/max), `auth_servers` (RADIUS/TACACS+/LDAP state). All follow the same defensive conventions.

- **`backend/firewallguard/tsr/normalize.py:298-307`** — `normalize_tsr()` is the dual-format entry point. `detect_tsr_format()` (line 95) distinguishes API vs GUI by comparing own-line `#…_START` markers to total count: if ≥10 total markers and ≤25% are on own lines, it's API format. `normalize_api_tsr()` (line 261) runs 6 reconstruction passes: (1) rejoin comma-broken lines, (2) collapse IPv6 split literals, (3) `_restore_markers()` puts section markers on own lines from a `sonicos_sections.txt` catalog, (4) `_reconstruct_blocks()` re-inserts record boundaries (table markers, dash headers, member lines, VPN/access-rule headers), (5) `_segment_kv()` re-segments run-on key:value pairs using a `sonicos_keys.txt` catalog via longest-suffix matching, (6) `_demerge_interfaces()` de-merges collapsed management interface lists. `_fixups()` re-spaces model/firmware tokens, numeric colons, and DH Group/VPN proposal tokens.

- **`backend/firewallguard/rules/engine.py:1-105`** — Core rule model: `Finding` dataclass with 20 fields including `rule_id, title, severity, category, description, evidence, business_impact, technical_impact, remediation, verification, risk_reduction, references, compliance, likelihood/impact/exposure (1-5), affected_count, object_name/type/detail`. `Finding.exploitability` property computes a composite score (weighted 40% likelihood, 35% exposure, 25% impact) mapped to Critical/High/Medium/Low bands. `Rule` dataclass wraps an id/title/severity/category + `check(snapshot) -> List[Finding]` callable, with exception-safe `run()`. `RuleRegistry` holds an ordered list, supports `retire()` for superseded rule IDs, a `rule(**meta)` decorator for registration, and `run_all(snapshot)` which returns findings sorted by severity order then rule ID.

- **`backend/firewallguard/rules/catalog.py:1-918`** — Core detection catalog with ~25 rules across management security, authentication, access rules, service configuration, VPN/IPsec, and security services. Compliance mappings to CIS Controls v8, NIST CSF 2.0, PCI DSS 4.0, ISO/IEC 27001:2022. Each rule is evidence-gated: findings are only emitted when the TSR explicitly shows the condition (e.g., `mgmt_on_wan` checks WAN interfaces intersect with management interface lists). All rules use `@registry.rule(...)` decorator.

- **`backend/firewallguard/rules/catalog_parity.py:1-910`** — Per-object parity rules (~32 checks across ACR, AOB, SVC, NAT, IPSEC, SEC, GAV, IPS, CFS, FW, AUTH, RAD, SNMP, MGMT, SSLVPN, WLAN, PERF, SYSTEM, DHCP families). Many are per-object: iterate over access rules/address objects/NAT policies/VPN policies and emit one finding each with `object_name`/`object_type`/`object_detail` populated. Examples: `acr_any_service` (WAN allow rules with Any service), `aob_unused` (unreferenced address objects), `svc_unused` (unreferenced service objects), `ipsec_weak_dh` (per-VPN-policy DH group check).

- **`backend/firewallguard/intelligence/correlation.py:1-92`** — `correlate(findings, firmware_intel)` implements deterministic rule-based attack path chaining. Hard constraints: any Critical finding caps score at 59 (grade F), any High at 79 (max C). Grades: 100=Secure, 90-99=A, 80-89=B, 70-79=C, 60-69=D, <60=F. Also provides `severity_breakdown()`, `category_breakdown()`, `exploitability_distribution()`.

- **`backend/firewallguard/analytics/drift.py:208-247`** — `detect_drift(previous_snapshot, current_snapshot)` compares 7 dimensions: access rules (keyed by `src_zone->dst_zone|service|src->dst|name`), NAT policies, VPN policies, security services (individual toggle comparisons with per-field severity), firmware version, administration settings (MFA, password policy), and interfaces (add/remove/re-address). - **`backend/firewallguard/pipeline.py:1-120`** — `analyze_text(text)` and `analyze_snapshot(snapshot)` orchestrate the full pipeline: (1) `parse_tsr()` produces snapshot, (2) `registry.run_all(snapshot)` runs all active rules, (3) optional system-filter callback applies CEL-based suppression, (4) optional `extra_findings_fn` injects DB-stored CEL rule results, (5) `get_intel().evaluate()` runs firmware PSIRT matching, (6) PSIRT findings are promoted to Finding objects, (7) `_apply_suppressions()` handles tenant-level disable/override, (8) `correlate()` builds attack paths, (9) `score_findings()` computes score/grade. - **`backend/firewallguard/report/generator.py:1-575`** — ReportLab-based PDF generation. `build_executive_pdf()` (line 232) produces a 1-page summary with score band, device info, posture summary, firmware advisory table, and attack path section. `build_technical_pdf()` (line 355) produces a detailed report with clickable finding index and per-finding detail cards (evidence, impact, remediation, verification, compliance). `build_comparison_pdf()` (line 410) compares two analysis runs for before/after assessment. `export_findings_csv()` and `export_json()` produce data exports. - **`backend/firewallguard/cli.py:1-80`** — Two subcommands: `analyze TSR.wri [--out OUTDIR]` runs full pipeline and optionally writes PDF/CSV/JSON reports; `drift OLD_TSR.wri NEW_TSR.wri [--json]` parses both and runs `detect_drift`. All outputs go to filesystem, no database required.

Mitigation: expand the key/section catalog coverage with fallback heuristics or automated discovery from the API export itself.
2. **Score anchoring** — The scoring caps (Critical→max 59, High→max 79) are hardcoded thresholds.
